cards.back: A **frameshift mutation** is an insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three. Every later codon is shifted and changed.
cards.hint: Think about how bases are grouped into codons when the sequence is read.

cards.front: How can changing one amino acid stop an enzyme from working?
cards.back: The amino acid order sets how the polypeptide folds, so the **tertiary structure** changes. The active site changes shape, so the substrate can no longer bind.
cards.hint: Follow the chain from amino acid order to folding to the active site.

cards.back: A **nonsense mutation** is a substitution that changes an amino acid codon into a stop codon. Translation ends early.
cards.hint: Compare the new codon with the old one.

cards.back: A **gene mutation** is a change in the DNA base sequence of a gene.
cards.hint: Think of a single wrong letter in a recipe.

cards.back: A **mutagen** is an agent, such as ionising radiation or certain chemicals, that increases the rate at which mutations occur.
cards.hint: Think about factors that make mutations more likely, not the mutations themselves.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to assume every gene mutation harms the organism?
cards.back: **Many** mutations have no effect on the protein, and a few may even be useful. Only some change the protein enough to cause harm.
A **deletion** is a gene mutation in which one or more bases are removed from the sequence.
A **codon** is a group of three adjacent bases in mRNA that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.
cards.hint: Think about how mRNA is read in groups.

cards.front: What does it mean for the genetic code to be degenerate?
cards.back: The genetic code is **degenerate** when most amino acids are specified by more than one codon.
cards.hint: Compare how many codons a single amino acid can have.

cards.back: A **silent mutation** is a gene mutation that does not change the amino acid sequence. The new codon still codes for the same amino acid, which relies on the degenerate code.
cards.hint: Consider what happens when a new codon is compared with the old one.

cards.back: A **missense mutation** is a substitution that changes one codon so that it specifies a different amino acid.

cards.front: Why can a substitution change at most one amino acid?
cards.back: A substitution alters only the codon that contains the changed base. Neighbouring codons stay the same, because codons are read one after another without overlaps.
cards.hint: Think about how codons are read along the mRNA.

cards.front: Which is more likely to shift every later codon: deleting 1 base or deleting 3 bases?
cards.back: Deleting **1 base** causes a frameshift, so every later codon changes. Deleting 3 bases keeps the reading frame, so only one codon and one amino acid are lost.
cards.hint: Think about how many codons would be regrouped in each case.

cards.back: Gene mutations arise **at random**, often when DNA is copied during replication. A few errors are not corrected by the cell.
